title: Seeking Christ at the Tomb
english: …of good things, and does not show the very image of the realities (Hebrews 10:1). Behind it the truth took its stand (Song of Songs 2:9), close by the place, and afterwards it shines out. Or else he spoke of the cutting (Song of Songs 2:12) as the cutting of the spiritual harvest, of which the Savior says, 'The harvest is plentiful' (Matthew 9:37).

'In the shelter of the rock, close by the outer wall' (Song of Songs 2:14). The outer wall shows safety: once you are there, he says, you will find help of every kind. 'Turn' (Song of Songs 2:17). She asks the bridegroom to leave the fruitless Synagogue and to come to those who have risen to heavenly height from a soul that was once sunken, brought low and given to idols.

'On my bed by night I sought' (Song of Songs 3:1). He means the women who came to the tomb of Jesus at early dawn on the first day of the week and did not find Him (Luke 24:1–3). So by 'on my bed' she means either 'from bed', or she calls the Lord's tomb her own bed, since in it we are buried with Him (Romans 6:4). But she did not find Him, for she heard, 'He is not here; for He has risen' (Matthew 28:6). And the angels who keep watch found her (Song of Songs 3:3), and she asks them too, 'Where have you laid the Lord?' (John 20:13). But when she had passed those she questioned, He met her, saying, 'Rejoice' (Matthew 28:9). That is why she says, 'Scarcely had I passed from them when I found Him, and I will not let Him go' (Song of Songs 3:4). For she took hold of His feet (Matthew 28:9) and heard, 'Do not touch Me' (John 20:17). By her mother's house he means the gathering of the apostles, to which she went and announced the good news of Christ's resurrection (John 20:18).

'Perfumed with myrrh and frankincense' (Song of Songs 3:6). Myrrh, when she has been buried with Him; frankincense, when she has risen with Him and come to share in His divinity. And the soul of the Church is perfumed not only with these, but also with the varied insights of knowledge. For one who divides things with the utmost precision and examines them finely down to the least detail could be called a kind of perfumer, grinding fine and reducing to powder all the fragrant sayings with which the bride is now said to be perfumed.

Perhaps, too, one who lives not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit (Romans 8:4), whose heart has in no way grown dull (Matthew 13:15), keeps the fragrance varied and of every kind, and makes a fragrance from all the things now called 'the powders of the perfumer' (Song of Songs 3:6).
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum canticorum (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.

This section opens mid-sentence: the previous one ends '…the Law, which casts the shadow of the things to come', and this one supplies the rest of Hebrews 10:1 ('of good things, not the very image of the realities'), so the English begins with an ellipsis. 'οὗ ὀπίσω' ('behind which') refers to the law as the wall of Song of Songs 2:9.
The lemma 'Ἐν σκέπῃ τῆς πέτρας, ἐχόμενα τοῦ προτειχίσματος' is printed twice in a row; the repeat is a printing slip and is translated once.

'Σμύρνα μὲν, ὅτε συντέθαπται διὰ τοῦ λιβάνου': the words 'διὰ τοῦ λιβάνου' ('through the frankincense') make no sense with myrrh and look corrupt (perhaps for 'through baptism', Romans 6:4). They are not rendered; the clause is given as 'Myrrh, when she has been buried with Him'.
'Ἐκράτησε γὰρ οὗτος πόδας αὐτοῦ': the masculine οὗτος does not fit the woman who is the subject; read as 'she took hold of His feet' (Matthew 28:9).

The last sentence runs across the section break ('εὐωδίαν ἀπὸ πάντων | ποιεῖ τῶν νῦν οὕτως ὀνομαζομένων κονιορτῶν μυρεψοῦ'); it is translated whole here, and the next section begins with the next sentence.
The stray '3' and the column number '69.1288' are print furniture and are not translated.
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum u02 rem early

title: The Bride Comes Up from the Desert
english: One might also say that the holy soul of the Church, once a child bereft of God, comes up from the gathering of the nations, 'from the desert' (Song of Songs 3:6): she leaves behind teachings, words and deeds that are empty of God, and rises to the things of God. Let the spiritual union, precious and divine, be understood as the gold (Song of Songs 3:10). For gold coated the ark in the desert too, inside and out (Exodus 25:11), to make the divine union plain. The purple (Song of Songs 3:10) rests upon the multitude of those called to the kingdom. And whenever anyone believes, he receives into his heart Christ, who is the precious pearl (Matthew 13:46).

And the litter, he says, was made from the daughters of Jerusalem out of love alone (Song of Songs 3:9–10): 'For God so loved the world that He sent His only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life' (John 3:16).

It is the Church from the nations that says, 'Go forth and see' (Song of Songs 3:11). He calls the day of the Passion 'the day of His wedding', the day on which He took the Church as His bride through His blood (Acts 20:28). Her silence (Song of Songs 4:1) signifies obedience in everything, as in the words, 'Be silent and listen, Israel' (Deuteronomy 27:9). Or else the two fawns, the moral and the doctrinal teaching, are the bride's two breasts (Song of Songs 4:5); those nourished from them look toward God with keen sight. By the lilies he means the fragrance of the apostolic and Gospel words, on which we feed until the end.

'Come from Lebanon, bride' (Song of Songs 4:8). He teaches us where the bride comes from, and that she comes out of idolatry. For Lebanon is a mountain full of idols. From there, he says, you will come; and you will pass through the law, for without knowing the law you were instructed in the mystery of Christ.

'You have given us heart, my sister, bride' (Song of Songs 4:9). That is, you have drawn us to long for you by a single word of confession, which you held rightly, seeing with your inner eyes. For it was by submitting to the ornament on your neck that you made the confession. These words are spoken to her by the friends of the bridegroom, the angelic powers, I mean. For the activity of sight is twofold: one kind sees the truth, while the other wanders among vain things. Since the bride's pure eye is open to the nature of the good alone, while the other lies idle, the friends therefore offer their praise to one of her eyes. They call her sister because of the kinship that comes through freedom from passion, and bride because of her union with the Word.
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum canticorum (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.
The Greek of this section opens with 'ποιεῖ τῶν νῦν οὕτως ὀνομαζομένων κονιορτῶν μυρεψοῦ', the end of a sentence translated whole in the previous section.
'τὸ τέκνον ποτὲ ἔρημον Θεοῦ' means 'once a child bereft of God' (genitive of separation), not 'a child of God'.

Song of Songs 3:9–10 LXX: Solomon's litter (φορεῖον) has a back of gold, a seat (ἐπίβασις) of purple, an inlaid interior, 'love from the daughters of Jerusalem'. Cyril's 'Ἐπιβαίνει δὲ πορφύρα' plays on ἐπίβασις; the pearl answers the inlaid stones (λιθόστρωτον).
John 3:16 is quoted with ἀπέστειλεν ('sent') where the Gospel has ἔδωκεν ('gave'); the English follows Cyril's wording.
Song of Songs 4:1 LXX reads 'apart from your silence' (σιωπήσεως) where the Hebrew has 'veil'; Cyril comments on the LXX. 'Σιώπα καὶ ἄκουε, Ἰσραήλ' is Deuteronomy 27:9 LXX.

'Ῥῖνα δὲ τῶν ἀποστολικῶν καὶ εὐαγγελικῶν λόγων τὴν εὐωδίαν, ἅπερ νεμόμεθα': the print reads Ῥῖνα ('nose'), but the neuter plural ἅπερ and the lemma 'that feed among the lilies' (Song of Songs 4:5) show the word must be Κρίνα ('lilies'); rendered 'lilies'.
ἐκαρδίωσας (Song of Songs 4:9) is rendered 'you have given us heart' here and in the next section, where Cyril glosses it as putting soul and mind into the friends.
ἀπάθεια is 'freedom from passion', not 'apathy'.

The last sentence runs across the section break ('∆ιττῆς γὰρ οὔσης τῆς ὀπτικῆς | ἐνεργείας … διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸν Λόγον συνάφειαν'); it is translated whole here, and the next section begins with the next sentence.
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum u02 rem mid

title: The Single Eye and the Locked Garden
english: Since, then, he says, your eye is one in that it looks toward the one, and your soul is one because it is not divided among differing dispositions, and the set of your neck is perfect, for it has taken the divine yoke upon itself, for this reason we confess that you have given us heart by these wonders (Song of Songs 4:9). This is what 'the ornament of your neck' means, namely the Lord's yoke (Matthew 11:29). That is, through yourself you have put into us a kind of soul and mind for perceiving the light. For in you, as in a mirror, we behold the Sun of righteousness (Malachi 4:2). And by saying it twice they lend credibility to what is said.

'A garden locked' (Song of Songs 4:12). It is shut to the world, but open to the heavenly bridegroom. And the spring is sealed (Song of Songs 4:12) with the Holy Spirit, with whom we are anointed after baptism. For the virtues are signified by the spices (Song of Songs 4:14). By the trees of Lebanon he means the prophets. The myrrh and aloes show that Christ, once buried, came into fellowship with the saints who had gone before; for He went down into Hades and brought them up.

'On the cross,' he says, 'accepting death for the sake of mankind'; but the heart keeps watch (Song of Songs 5:2), in that as God He plundered Hades. That is: what has your beloved done, or what do you have from your beloved (Song of Songs 5:9)? By the lips dripping myrrh (Song of Songs 5:13) he means lips that confess His death. 'His legs are pillars of marble' (Song of Songs 5:15). These might also be bases, for those who are being built are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20). In due order, after the belly (Song of Songs 5:14), he praises the legs, which he says are pillars of marble set on bases of gold (Song of Songs 5:15).
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum u02 rem close
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 69; Fragmenta in Canticum canticorum (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.
The Greek of this section opens with 'ἐνεργείας … συνάφειαν', the end of a sentence translated whole in the previous section.
'ἐν τῷ 69.1289 πρὸς τὸ ἒν βλέπειν': '69.1289' is a PG column number set inside the phrase 'ἐν τῷ πρὸς τὸ ἓν βλέπειν' ('in looking toward the one'); it is not translated.
The parenthesis 'τοῦτο γὰρ τὸ ἐνθέματι τραχήλου σου, εἶτ' οὖν ὁ τοῦ Κυρίου ζυγός' is given as a separate sentence after the main clause for readability.
'διὰ δὲ τῆς δευτερώσεως': Song of Songs 4:9 LXX says 'ἐκαρδίωσας ἡμᾶς' twice; the friends' repetition lends weight to their words.

'Ἐν τῷ σταυρῷ, φησὶ, τὸν ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων ἀναδεχόμενος θάνατον' has no main verb: the catena has lost the lemma 'I sleep' of Song of Songs 5:2 ('I sleep, but my heart is awake'). The fragment is kept as it stands.
ἀδελφιδός is rendered 'beloved', as in English versions of the Song, not 'brother'. κνῆμαι are legs, not knees.

The last sentence runs across the section break ('ἅς φησι στύλους εἶναι | μαρμαρίνους τεθεμελιωμένους ἐπὶ βάσεις χρυσᾶς'); it is translated whole here, and the next section begins with the next sentence.
The stray '4' at the end of the Greek section is a print number and is not translated.
